newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says he's not worried about McDougal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says he's not worried about McDougal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Friday he was "not worried at all" at the possibility that a former partner in the failed Whitewater land venture, James McDougal, might provide some damaging evidence against him.

McDougal was sentenced to three years in prison on Monday after agreeing to cooperate with Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr. He had faced up to 81 years in prison for his conviction last May on 18 counts of fraud and conspiracy.
He later hinted that he gave Starr information that could implicate the president and first lady, saying "I think they should be deeply concerned."

McDougal reportedly reversed his earlier statements and told investigators that in 1986, as governor of Arkansas, Clinton pressured a banker to extend an illegal $300,000 loan to McDougal's former wife, Susan McDougal.
Clinton denied the allegation under oath during the McDougals' trial last year. Susan McDougal was sentenced to two years in prison for her part in winning the fraudulent loan.
However, she has refused to cooperate with Starr and is serving a contempt of court sentence for refusing to testify before a grand jury.

McDougal said he gave Starr information because Clinton had failed to pardon Susan McDougal. "I really thought he would pardon her. That was a big factor in my decision," he said. "I just got sick and tired of lying for the fellow."

Asked at a news conference if he was concerned, Clinton said tersely: "No." Asked to elaborate, he added: "We did not do anything wrong. We had nothing to do with all these business matters that were the subject of the trial. No, I'm not worried at all."
Clinton also denied any link between separate meetings in 1994 he had with Indonesian businessman James Riady and former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell, an old friend from Arkansas.

Critics have suggested that $400,000 Hubbell got for work he did for the Riady family of Indonesia and others after he left the Justice Department amounted to hush money to keep him quiet about Whitewater.
